constraints.evidence: Slide 18 sizes six actions against the 3.0% target ($43.9M, 'about $1.5M above 3.0%') and shows 2.9% without the three long-lease exits. But the 3.1% divides by $1,412M of post-exit sales. On FY2025 sales it is about 2.9%, below the ~$45.1M the checklist needs. The slide title still says '3.1% margin on FY2025 sales'.

Slide 18/20: 'promotions, the delivery fee and shrink add about $17.9M, taking operating income to $33.2M against the $20M floor'. Closures are excluded from the covenant test, which is correct. The $17.9M is a full run-rate figure at FY2025 sales: no part-year phasing and no downside case against $20M.

'three long-lease exits, at $7.5M of the $25M limit' appears in the executive summary, slide 17 and slide 20. Slide 12 says '$19.1M ... before one-time costs', and no other one-time costs (rollout, severance, hours redeployment) are sized against the cap.
Slide 17 separates six stores (leases end by 2027, 'Board vote Not needed', no exit cost) from three stores ('Board vote Required', $7.5M). The next steps bring the three exits to a board vote.

The plan keeps home delivery ('keep home delivery', slide 15 title; 'Roll out the tested fee; steer orders to click-and-collect'). The owners' commitment is never named, and an exit-delivery option is never argued against it.

Slide 6 notes 'a further 4% rise is due in 2027'. Slide 18 says 'a 4% rise on the whole store-labor bill would cost $7.3M' against $1.5M of headroom, but also 'No wage, rent or delivery-rate inflation ... assumed'. The headline 3.1% ignores it, and the document's own numbers show it would erase the target.

Slide 14: -$10.4M after delivery cost and 70% cannibalisation. It corrects the 6.1% claim, notes $13.80 delivery cost against a $3.10 fee, and shows home share rising from 45% to 58%. The 3% provider rise (~$0.3M) is named but left out of the headline.
Slide 9: '$14.5M saving − $10M more shrink (0.67 pp) = $4.5M net ... before lost sales'. Slides 8 and 19 use the shrink-by-quartile gradient (3.1% vs 2.3%) to reject the cut.

Slide 12 gives 'Risk: stores within three miles of a ValuMart had comparable sales of −4.2% ... hold their key prices'. The $10.5M headline is gross of any lost sales. 'Not counted: vendor funding back toward 55%' means vendor funding is not assumed to recover.

Slide 17: $3.1M loss removed + $3.5M transfer contribution = $6.6M for all nine. Six stores give $4.4M at no cost, three give $2.2M for $7.5M (3.4-year payback), and $88.5M of sales is lost. Slide 18 says the exits come after the covenant test, and the covenant check excludes them.

alternatives.evidence: The 8% cut is sized at $4.5M net of $10M extra shrink (slide 9), with the Q1-vs-Q4 shrink evidence, and rejected. The recommendation redeploys hours to high-shrink stores. A smaller or targeted cut is not tested, and neither is a shrink-tracked pilot. The $4.5M is still a positive saving that is not weighed against the plan.

The fee rollout half-measure is sized (+$2.8M, loss falls to $7.6M) and adopted, and the contract renewal is used to resist the 3% rise. Exiting home delivery while keeping click-and-collect is never named or sized. Slide 15 only says 'Delivery still loses money: about $9.04 per delivered order'.

The category team's 'promotions work' case is rejected ('counts sales, not profit'), citing 38% of events losing money and price perception rising from 33% to 41%. A full rollback to 24% is adopted, with 'drop money-losing events first'. Pruning alone is not sized against the full rollback, and the −4.2% ValuMart traffic risk is not netted off.

Slide 17 compares six at expiry ($4.4M, no cost, no vote), three long-lease ($2.2M for $7.5M, 3.4-year payback) and all nine ($6.6M). Slide 18 shows 2.9% without the three. 'Close none' is implied only by the baseline.

sensitivities.evidence: Slide 9 gives one scenario (+0.67 pp shrink → $10M, net $4.5M), flagged as an 'upper bound'. There is no range, no break-even (the +1.0 pp that wipes out the saving) and no FY2026 covenant threshold for management's plan. The plan's own $4.5M shrink gain has no sensitivity.

'The test was small, so the rollout should be staged and tracked' and 'lost online sales follow the survey: 70% ... 30%'. The cannibalisation rate is never varied (no 50% or 29% break-even case). The fee-response range is not shown either, and there is no exit-delivery value.

Slide 12 names the ValuMart risk (−4.2% vs +1.1% comps) and the response 'hold their key prices'. It does not show the sales-loss rate that erases the $10.5M (~3.5% of sales), or how much of the saving comes from the 38% of losing events.

overclaim.quote: Six actions reach a 3.1% margin; promotions, the delivery fee and shrink start first / "Together, six actions would lift operating income to about $44M, a 3.1% margin on FY2025 sales"

omissions: No FY2026 phasing or downside case for the $20M covenant. The $33.2M assumes full run-rate effects of promotions, the fee rollout and the shrink fix inside the first year. Slide 12 labels the same figures 'by FY2028'.

The 3.1% headline uses a post-exit sales denominator ($1,412M) but is labelled 'on FY2025 sales' (about 2.9% there). It ignores the 2027 wage rise, which the document itself says would cost $7.3M against $1.5M of headroom. No levers or contingency are offered to cover that gap.
Exiting home delivery while keeping click-and-collect is never sized or argued against the owners' 'keep delivery' commitment, although e-commerce is the largest single driver of the decline.

Execution costs of the plan are not sized against the $25M cap or the profit figures: extra labor to staff produce rotation and receiving, the fee rollout, vendor renegotiation, and any exit costs for the six stores.
The document does not tie the plan to the covenant or the 3.0% target in a downside case (for example ValuMart traffic loss, or smaller fee-test and shrink effects).
unsupported_assumptions: "Shrink: from 2.6% to the best quartile's 2.3% of sales by moving hours to receiving and produce rotation" ($4.5M). It assumes the whole quartile gap is caused by hours and can be closed at no labor cost. That sits awkwardly with slide 9, which calls attributing all shrink to staffing an upper bound.
"5 percentage points of sales back to regular price, each dollar earning 14 percentage points more margin" ($10.5M). It assumes none of the volume is lost to ValuMart or to price perception.
"Private label: 0.75 percentage points of share a year for three years" ($4.1M). It extrapolates the FY2023–25 trend with no driver, and it ignores any interaction with the promotions rollback.
"The 4-store, 10-week test holds chain-wide: delivered orders −9%, click-and-collect +14%, online sales −2%, fee $6.40". This scales a small test to $2.8M a year.
"six and three pro-rated by store count" ($4.4M / $2.2M). The pack gives no store-level split, so the 3.4-year payback and the 'needed to reach 3.0%' claim rest on pro-rating.
"No wage, rent or delivery-rate inflation and no sales growth assumed". The plan's 3.1% depends on this, yet the document names the 2027 wage rise and the 3% delivery rate rise as real.
